name: The public sphere, print, and the periodical
description: The formation of a reading public reached by daily papers, weeklies, reviews and circulating libraries, and the literature that made criticism, morality and politics a matter of general conversation.

name: Wit, ridicule, and the war against dullness
description: The satiric conviction that stupidity, pedantry and false taste are public evils to be punished by laughter, and the personification of Dulness as a power in the state.

name: Sympathy, benevolence, and the moral sense
description: The theory and practice of fellow-feeling as the foundation of obligation: the tear, the palpitation, the distress scene, and the imagination of another's situation as the test of virtue.

name: Taste, decorum, and the rules of art
description: The argument about whether writing is governed by imitable rules drawn from the ancients, by an innate faculty of taste, or by native genius and its irregularities.

name: Commerce, luxury, and commercial society
description: The moral and literary problem of a society made by trade: opulence, credit, the corruption of independency, the new politeness of commerce, and its critics.

name: Liberty, corruption, and the decline of nations
description: The country and commonwealth language of free government, ministerial corruption, standing armies and the fall of states, extended by the philosophical history of republics and empires.

name: Death, mourning, and the graveyard meditation
description: The deliberate cultivation of the thought of death, the funeral and the unknown dead as the discipline by which the living reader is instructed.

name: The sublime, terror, and the ruin
description: The aesthetic of overwhelming power, obscurity and awful delight, and the pleasure taken in ruins, vastness and the machinery of fear.

name: Primitive genius and national poetry
description: The belief that poetry is oldest and best when it is wild, inspired and national: the bard, the fragment, the ballad, and the argument about authenticity.

name: Women's education and intellectual friendship
description: The claim to learning, the society of letters, the conversation and the correspondence through which women made an intellectual public for themselves.

name: Seduction and the betrayed heroine
description: The plot of a woman's vulnerability to artifice and to the law of a family without remedy, and the social analysis of honour, chastity and abandonment.

name: The slave trade and abolition
description: The testimony, argument and appeal against the trade in enslaved people, and the exposure of commerce, empire and Christian conscience to one another.

name: Enthusiasm and the disease of the imagination
description: The diagnosis of religious frenzy, superstition and credulity as a malady of the mind, and the literary uses both of the enthusiast's voice and of the sceptic's irony.

name: Evangelical experience and assurance
description: The narrative of conversion, the evidence of things felt, the doctrine of assurance, and the joy and terror of a religion addressed to the common person.

name: Rural labour, depopulation, and the deserted village
description: The lament for enclosure, depopulation, the decay of the country parish and the labouring poor, and the idealisation or rejection of rustic life.

name: Poverty, dependence, and the professional writer
description: The experience and the rhetoric of the Grub Street and hired-pen economy: patronage failing, the bookseller rising, and the writer's independence asserted in print.

name: Self-knowledge and the philosophy of the mind
description: The empirical examination of the understanding, the association of ideas, personal identity, memory and the passions, carried from the treatise into the diary, the novel and the meditation.

name: Jacobitism, loyalty, and the '45
description: The political allegiance and the song, broadside and elegy produced by the exiled house of Stuart, the risings of 1715 and 1745, and their suppression.

name: The literature of the nations: Scotland, Ireland, and Wales
description: Writing that asserts or invents a national literary tradition after the Union: the Gaelic and Welsh revivals, the collected and imitated songs, and the antiquarian defence of the Celtic.

name: Progress, decay, and the philosophy of history
description: The great question of whether societies and religions advance or degenerate, told through the stages of commerce, the fall of empires and the history of Christianity.

name: Politeness, fashion, and the codes of conduct
description: The discipline of manners, the theatre of fashion, the etiquette of the assembly and the tea-table, and the moral criticism of politeness as a substitute for virtue.

name: Childhood, innocence, and education
description: The new conception of the child as a being with its own rights and its own capacity, worked out in the school book, the tale, the conduct literature and the poem.
